mainTopic: Partners dividing a courtyard: היזק ראיה, binding the agreement with a קנין, the wall's building materials and thickness, and the אמה טרקסין
overview: This amud opens with the last words of the first version of the discussion about the משנה's wall between partners. Then the גמרא gives a second version. It asks whether מחיצה means 'division' or 'wall', and whether היזק ראיה (damage from being seen) counts as real damage. After a back-and-forth about the wording, the 'division' reading stands. רבי יוחנן explains that the משנה is about a courtyard too small to be divided by force, which is split only when both partners agree. Our משנה teaches that a real wall is then required, and a later משנה is needed for its rule that holy books are never divided. The גמרא then asks why an agreement binds the partners at all. It answers that they made a קנין on specific sides of the courtyard, or, according to רב אשי, each took possession of his own part. Next the גמרא defines the building materials גויל, גזית, כפיסין and לבנים, and רב אשי teaches that these meanings come from tradition. אביי learns that the gap between a wall's rows is a טפח, and the גמרא discusses how thick a wall must be, using the אמה טרקסין of the first מקדש. The amud ends with a dispute over whether the second מקדש was 'greater' in its building, and that dispute continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Closing words of the first version: so I can hide from you
steps.stepSummary: The tail end of the first version's discussion. The partner's claim ends with the reason he wants a proper wall: so that he can be hidden from his neighbor.
steps.simpleTranslation: …so that I can be hidden from you.
steps.whatsHappening: These two words finish an argument that began before this section, in the first version of the discussion. The partner explains that he wants a real wall so he can be hidden from his neighbor's eyes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key idea is privacy. A partner can demand a proper wall because a flimsy divider would not stop the other partner from seeing him. This closes the first version, and the גמרא now moves to a second version.

keyTerms.meaning: So that I can be hidden / keep private
Privacy, being hidden (the root of the word used here)

phrases.english: so that I can be hidden from you.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the argument of the first version from before this section.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives the privacy reason behind the partner's demand for a solid wall
steps.terutzMaskana: The partner wants a real wall so he can be hidden from his neighbor.

steps.title: Second version: מחיצה means a division, so seeing is damage
steps.stepSummary: In the second version, the Sages first assume that מחיצה in the משנה means 'division,' based on a פסוק. Read that way, once the partners want to divide the courtyard, a wall is built even against one partner's will. That proves היזק ראיה counts as damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another version tells it this way: They assumed that מחיצה means 'a division,' as the פסוק says, 'And the division of the congregation was.' So the משנה means: once they wanted to divide the courtyard, we build the wall even against their will. This shows that damage from seeing counts as damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts over with a second version of the discussion. Here the first assumption is that מחיצה means 'division,' and from that the גמרא proves that היזק ראיה is real damage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If מחיצה means 'division,' the partners only agreed to split the courtyard, not to build a wall. Yet the משנה says they build a wall anyway, even against someone's will. The only reason to force a wall is to stop the partners from seeing each other, so seeing must count as damage.

keyTerms.meaning: They assumed (an early assumption the גמרא may later question)
Damage caused by being seen (loss of privacy)

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'they wanted' (רצו) means they wanted to divide the courtyard, not that they agreed to build a wall. The wall itself is forced on them.
steps.whyThisMatters: Whether היזק ראיה counts as damage decides if one neighbor can force another to build a wall for privacy.

phrases.english: Another version says it this way:
They assumed: what does "מחיצה" mean? A division,
as it is written: "And the division of the congregation was";
phrases.notes: במדבר 31:43

phrases.aramaic: וְכֵיוָן דְּרָצוּ – בּוֹנִין אֶת הַכּוֹתֶל בְּעַל כּוֹרְחָן,
phrases.english: and once they wanted [to divide], they build the wall against their will,
apparently, damage from seeing is called damage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new version of the whole discussion, separate from the first version that just ended.
steps.raayaObject: היזק ראיה שמיה היזק (damage from seeing counts as damage)
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה, read so that מחיצה means 'division' (based on the פסוק in במדבר), which forces a wall against a partner's will

steps.title: Maybe מחיצה means a wall, as in the vineyard משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back: מחיצה could just as well mean 'a wall.' It proves this from a משנה about a breached vineyard fence, which uses the same word.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say instead that מחיצה means 'a wall.' As we learned: if a vineyard's fence broke, the neighbor says to the owner, 'Fence it.' If it broke again, he says again, 'Fence it.' If the owner gave up on it and did not fence it, he has made the crops forbidden and must pay for the loss.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the reading from step 2. It says מחיצה might mean 'wall,' and brings a משנה where the word clearly means a fence.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the vineyard משנה, מחיצת הכרם clearly means a physical fence between the vineyard and the neighbor's grain field. If the same meaning applies in our משנה, then 'they wanted' means they wanted to build a wall. That changes what the משנה proves.

keyTerms.meaning: As we learned in a משנה
Made forbidden (here, the crops become forbidden as כלאי הכרם)

phrases.english: Say instead: what does "מחיצה" mean? A wall;
as we learned: a vineyard fence that was breached —
he says to him: "Fence it."
If it was breached again — he says to him: "Fence it."
If he gave up on it and did not fence it —
he has made it forbidden, and he is responsible for the loss.
phrases.notes: Literally 'sanctified,' but here it means the grain and grapes became forbidden as כלאי הכרם.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges how step 2 read the word מחיצה.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the assumption that מחיצה must mean 'division'
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The word מחיצה can mean a physical wall, as it does in the vineyard משנה, so the proof is not forced.

steps.title: If they had to agree, seeing is not damage
steps.stepSummary: If מחיצה means 'wall,' then the wall is built only because both partners wanted it. Without that agreement, nobody is forced to build, so היזק ראיה would not count as damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the reason they build is that they both wanted it. But if they did not want it, we do not force him. This shows that damage from seeing is not called damage!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its objection by drawing the opposite conclusion from the משנה. Read this way, היזק ראיה is not damage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once 'they wanted' means 'they wanted a wall,' the משנה only applies when both partners agree to build. If one partner refuses, he cannot be forced, even though the other can see into his space. So the משנה now seems to teach that seeing is not real damage, the opposite of step 2.
steps.whatToRemember: In the second version, everything depends on the word מחיצה. If it means 'division,' the משנה proves היזק ראיה is damage. If it means 'wall,' the משנה suggests היזק ראיה is not damage.
steps.confusionAlert: This is not the final ruling. The גמרא is only showing that the משנה cannot prove the first side, because a second reading leads to the opposite result.

phrases.english: And the reason [they build] is that they wanted to,

phrases.aramaic: הָא לֹא רָצוּ – אֵין מְחַיְּיבִין אוֹתוֹ,
phrases.english: but if they did not want to — we do not obligate him,

phrases.aramaic: אַלְמָא הֶיזֵּק רְאִיָּה לָאו שְׁמֵיהּ הֶיזֵּק!
phrases.english: apparently, damage from seeing is not called damage!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from step 3's reading, which turns step 2's proof upside down.
steps.kashyaTarget: The proof in step 2 that היזק ראיה שמיה היזק
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If מחיצה means 'wall,' the משנה requires both partners to agree, so a refusing partner is not forced to build. That implies seeing is not damage, so the משנה cannot prove the opposite.

steps.title: If it means 'wall,' the wording should be 'build it'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the reading of מחיצה as 'wall,' since the משנה then repeats itself awkwardly.
steps.simpleTranslation: If מחיצה means a wall, why does the משנה go on to say 'they build the wall'? It should have said 'they build it'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the reading from Step 3, which says מחיצה means 'wall.' If that were true, the משנה's wording sounds repetitive.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says the partners wanted to make a מחיצה, and then that 'they build the כותל.' If מחיצה already means a wall, the second phrase should just say 'build it.' Using a new word suggests that מחיצה means something else, namely 'division.'

keyTerms.meaning: If so: introduces a problem that follows from the current claim

phrases.english: If so, "they build the wall"?!
It should have said "they build it"!
phrases.notes: Since the wall was already mentioned (as מחיצה), the משנה could have just said 'it.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the 'wall' reading that Steps 3-4 relied on.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A משנה would not repeat the noun with a different word; 'build it' would be enough.

steps.title: If it means 'division,' the wording should be 'to divide'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא turns the same kind of wording challenge against the 'division' reading.
steps.simpleTranslation: So what, does מחיצה mean 'division'? If so, why does the משנה say 'they wished to make a division'? It should have said 'they wished to divide'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks whether the other reading, 'division,' works any better. It finds a wording problem there too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If מחיצה means 'a division,' the phrase 'to make a division' is wordy. The plain verb 'to divide' (לחצות) would be more natural, so this reading also has a wording problem.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, what? Asks what the alternative is

phrases.english: Rather, what does it mean? A division?
If so, "who wished to make a division"?!
It should have said "who wished to divide"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 5's push toward 'division' by showing that reading has its own wording problem.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'Make a division' is a roundabout phrase when the simple verb 'divide' exists.

steps.title: People really do say 'let's make a division'
steps.stepSummary: The 'division' reading is defended: the משנה is just using everyday speech.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is how people talk: 'Come, let's make a division.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers Step 6. 'Make a division' is ordinary speech, so the 'division' reading survives.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem in Step 6 was only about style. Since people commonly say 'let's make a division,' the משנה can use that phrase. The 'division' reading still stands, and the 'wall' reading still has Step 5's problem.

keyTerms.meaning: As people say: an appeal to everyday speech

phrases.english: As people say:
Come, let us make a division.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 6's challenge to the 'division' reading.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Make a division' is too wordy to be what the משנה meant.
steps.terutzMaskana: It is normal speech, so מחיצה can mean 'division.'
steps.whatToRemember: The גמרא now leans toward reading מחיצה as 'division,' which supports the idea from Step 2 that היזק ראיה counts as damage.

steps.title: Why does the משנה need both partners to want it?
steps.stepSummary: If היזק ראיה is real damage, a partner should be forced to build even if the partners did not want to divide.
steps.simpleTranslation: If being seen counts as damage, why does the משנה speak only of a case where they wanted to divide? Even if they did not want to, a wall should be required!
steps.whatsHappening: Now that the 'division' reading stands, the גמרא raises a problem with it. If היזק ראיה is damage, why does the משנה mention 'they wanted' at all?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Real damage should be stopped no matter what the partners want. So the condition 'רצו' (they wanted) looks unnecessary. The גמרא asks why the משנה limits the case this way.

keyTerms.meaning: Damage caused by being seen (loss of privacy)
Why specifically? Why mention this case?

phrases.english: And if damage from being seen is called damage,
why specifically 'they wished'?
Even if they did not wish, the wall should be required too!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי הֶיזֵּק רְאִיָּה שְׁמֵיהּ הֶיזֵּק מַאי אִירְיָא רָצוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the 'division' reading confirmed in Step 7 and challenges its result.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the משנה shows היזק ראיה is damage
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If it were damage, the condition 'they wanted' would be needless.

steps.title: The משנה is about a courtyard too small to divide by force
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן explains that the courtyard is too small to be split by force, so it is split only if both partners agree.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אסי said in the name of רבי יוחנן: our משנה is about a courtyard too small to have the rule of forced division, and that is why it needs both partners to want it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers Step 8. The 'they wanted' is about agreeing to divide, not about building the wall.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A small courtyard cannot be divided unless both partners agree. So 'רצו' is needed for the division itself. Once they divide, a wall is required because of היזק ראיה.

keyTerms.meaning: The rule allowing one partner to force a division

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי אַסִּי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Asi said in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan:
Our mishna is where the courtyard does not have the rule of division,
phrases.notes: The courtyard is too small for each partner to get the minimum share, so nobody can force a split.

phrases.english: and it applies only where they wished.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 8 by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'They wanted' refers to wanting a wall, so a wall is not otherwise required.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'They wanted' refers to dividing a small courtyard. Once they divide, a wall is required.
steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אַסִּי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשְׁנָתֵנוּ כְּשֶׁאֵין בָּהּ דִּין חֲלוּקָה
steps.whyThisMatters: This answer keeps the proof from Step 2 alive: היזק ראיה still counts as damage.

steps.title: We already learned this in another משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what our משנה adds, since a later משנה already teaches that a small courtyard is divided when both partners agree.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the משנה teaching us, that a courtyard too small to divide may be divided if both want to? We already learned that: 'When does this rule apply? When they do not both want it. But when both want it, they divide even a smaller courtyard.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי יוחנן's answer. On his reading, our משנה seems to repeat a rule taught elsewhere.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A later משנה states that partners may divide even a small courtyard if both agree. So if our משנה only teaches that, it adds nothing new. The גמרא wants to know what it adds.

keyTerms.meaning: What is it teaching us? What new point does it add?
Less than this (smaller than the minimum size)

phrases.english: What is it teaching us?
That when it does not have the rule of division,
if they wish, they divide?!
We already learned this: When does this apply?
phrases.notes: This quotes a משנה later in this מסכת, about the minimum size a courtyard needs to be split by force.

phrases.english: When they do not both wish to divide,
but when both of them wish,
they divide even if it is smaller than this!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in Step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's reading of our משנה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A משנה should not repeat a rule that another משנה already states.

steps.title: Our משנה teaches that a real wall is required
steps.stepSummary: The other משנה could be read as allowing a flimsy divider. Our משנה teaches that a solid wall is needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: If we only had that other משנה, I would think a small courtyard may be divided with just a flimsy divider. Our משנה teaches that a real wall is needed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers Step 10. Our משנה adds something new: the kind of divider required.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The later משנה only says that the partners may divide. Our משנה adds that they must build a real כותל, which blocks the view. This new point fits the idea that היזק ראיה counts as damage.

keyTerms.meaning: A flimsy divider made of pegs or stakes

phrases.english: If we learned it from there, I would have said
that even if it is smaller than this,
they divide with a mere peg divider;
it teaches us here: a wall.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 10 by showing what our משנה adds.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing a new detail (the kind of divider)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A small courtyard divided by agreement needs only a flimsy peg divider.
steps.whatToRemember: By agreement, partners may divide a courtyard that is too small to split by force. Once they divide, they must build a real wall, not just a marker. This fits the view that היזק ראיה is damage.

steps.title: Then why is the other משנה needed?
steps.stepSummary: Since our משנה teaches more, the other משנה seems unnecessary.
steps.simpleTranslation: Then let the משנה teach only this one and not teach that one!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא flips the question. Our משנה teaches everything the later one does and more, so why have the later one at all?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Our משנה teaches both that the partners may divide and that they must build a wall. The later משנה seems to add nothing. So the גמרא asks why it was taught.

phrases.english: Then let it teach this one
and not teach that one!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the answer of Step 11 to challenge the need for the other משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for the later משנה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If our משנה covers everything, the later one is repetitive.

steps.title: The other משנה was needed for its rule about holy books
steps.stepSummary: The later משנה was taught for its last clause: holy books are not divided even if both partners want to divide them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Its last clause was needed: 'And holy writings may not be divided, even if both partners want to divide them.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers Step 12. The other משנה's real new point is in its final line, about holy books.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The later משנה lists items and when they are divided. Its last clause teaches something new: a holy book is never cut apart, even if both partners agree. The earlier lines were included to lead up to this rule.

keyTerms.meaning: The last clause of a משנה
It was needed for him (the תנא)

phrases.english: The last clause was necessary for him:
"And holy writings,
even if both of them wish,
they may not divide them."
phrases.notes: He means books written together on one scroll, which would have to be cut apart.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The other source is needed for a different clause
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The later משנה is repetitive and unneeded.
steps.terutzMaskana: It is needed for its final rule about holy books.
steps.whatToRemember: Both משניות are needed. Ours teaches that a real wall is required. The later one teaches that holy books are never divided, even if both partners agree.

steps.title: Another version: why can't a partner simply back out?
steps.stepSummary: In the alternative version, the גמרא asks: if the partners only agreed to divide, why can't one of them retract?
steps.simpleTranslation: Another version: And if they wanted to divide, so what? Let him back out!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a second version of the earlier discussion. It asks why an agreement to divide should force anyone to build a wall, since a partner could just change his mind.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this version the question is not about how big the courtyard is. It is about how binding the agreement is. A spoken agreement alone does not seem strong enough to force someone to pay for a stone wall.

keyTerms.meaning: Another version of the same discussion
So what? What difference does it make?
Let him retract or change his mind

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new topic. It is a second way of telling the same back-and-forth as steps 8-13, so expect the same pattern again.

phrases.english: Another version:
phrases.notes: This whole passage, up to the closing bracket a few lines down, is in round brackets. Some versions of the גמרא leave it out.

phrases.english: And if they wanted to divide, so what?
Let him retract!
phrases.notes: He means the partner who no longer wants to build the wall.

steps.triggerLanguage: לִישָּׁנָא אַחֲרִינָא: וְכִי רָצוּ מַאי הָוֵי? לִיהְדַּר בֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a second version of the discussion in steps 8-13. It takes the 'division' reading settled in step 7 and asks a different question about it.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that partners who wanted to divide a small courtyard must build a wall.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Wanting to divide is only an agreement in words, and a person should be able to take that back.

steps.title: They made a formal act of acquisition
steps.stepSummary: רב אסי in the name of רבי יוחנן answers that the case is where the partners made a קנין, so neither one can back out.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אסי said in the name of רבי יוחנן: The case is where they made a formal act of acquisition with each other, and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן answers the question. The משנה is talking about partners who sealed their agreement with a קנין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A קנין turns a spoken agreement into a binding commitment. Once that is done, neither partner can retract, so each one can be forced to build the wall.

keyTerms.meaning: They made a formal act of acquisition with him, which binds the agreement
A formal act that makes a deal legally binding

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב אַסִּי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rav Asi said that Rabbi Yochanan said:
The case is where they made an act of acquisition with him, etc.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אַסִּי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: בְּשֶׁקָּנוּ מִיָּדוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 14.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A partner could take back a spoken agreement.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה speaks of a case with a קנין, which cannot be taken back.

steps.title: Why not teach the bigger case?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the משנה taught a small courtyard where both agreed, instead of a large courtyard where a wall can be forced even without agreement.
steps.simpleTranslation: Instead of teaching us a courtyard that is too small to be divided, where they both agreed, let it teach us a courtyard big enough to be divided, even where they did not both agree!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the משנה chose this case. A large courtyard that can be divided by force seems like a stronger case to teach.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a wall can be forced even when one partner objects, that seems like the bigger lesson. So why did the משנה pick the case where both partners agreed?

keyTerms.meaning: Big enough that division can be forced, even if one partner objects

phrases.english: Instead of teaching us about a courtyard that is not subject to forced division
provided that they wanted to divide,
let it teach us about one that is subject to forced division
even though they did not both want to!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the answer and now asks why the משנה chose this case.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A case where the wall is forced against a partner's will seems to teach more.

steps.title: Without our משנה we would think agreement does not force a wall
steps.stepSummary: Had the משנה taught only the large courtyard, we would think that in a small courtyard nobody can be forced to build a wall, even after they both agreed. So the משנה teaches this case.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it had taught us only a courtyard big enough to be divided, even when they did not both agree, I would have thought: a courtyard too small to be divided, even if they agreed, still no wall can be forced. That is why the משנה teaches us this case.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the large-courtyard case would leave out something important. The משנה needs the small-courtyard case to teach that an agreement with a קנין also forces a wall.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Forcing a wall in a large courtyard comes from the law of division. We might have thought that only that law can force a wall, and an agreement never can. The משנה shows that an agreement sealed with a קנין also obligates a proper wall.

keyTerms.meaning: I would have thought (a mistaken first assumption)
So it teaches us (the lesson the text comes to teach)

phrases.aramaic: אִי אַשְׁמְעִינַן בְּיֵשׁ בָּהּ דִּין חֲלוּקָהּ –
phrases.english: If it had taught us about one subject to forced division
even though they did not both want to,

phrases.aramaic: הֲוָה אָמֵינָא: שֶׁאֵין בָּהּ דִּין חֲלוּקָהּ –
phrases.english: I would have said: one not subject to forced division
even if they wanted, also not;
phrases.notes: He means that no one could be forced to build a proper wall.

phrases.english: So it teaches us otherwise.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי אַשְׁמְעִינַן בְּיֵשׁ בָּהּ דִּין חֲלוּקָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 16.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: In a small courtyard, an agreement could never force someone to build a wall.
steps.terutzMaskana: An agreement with a קנין does force a proper wall, even in a small courtyard.

steps.title: The later משנה already teaches this
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: the later משנה already says that partners divide a small courtyard when both want to. Isn't that about a wall too?
steps.simpleTranslation: But can you really say that? The later clause teaches: When does this apply? When they do not both want to divide. But when they both want to, they divide. Isn't that talking about a wall?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer just given. A later משנה seems to already teach that agreement leads to division with a wall.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the later משנה already teaches that a wall is required when both partners agree, then our משנה adds nothing new. That would undo the answer of step 17.

keyTerms.meaning: The later clause of a משנה

phrases.english: But can you really say that?!
Doesn't the later clause teach:
phrases.notes: This is the משנה later in this פרק, on 11a.

phrases.english: When does this apply? When they do not both want to divide,
but when they both want to, they divide.
What, isn't that referring to a wall?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי מָצֵית אָמְרַתְּ הָכִי? וְהָא קָתָנֵי סֵיפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 17 from another משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that only our משנה teaches that agreement requires a wall.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The later משנה seems to teach the same thing, so our משנה would add nothing.

steps.title: The later משנה is about a light partition
steps.stepSummary: The later משנה only means a flimsy partition, not a real wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it refers to a mere light partition.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the later משנה does not mean a real wall. It could be speaking about a simple, flimsy divider.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the later משנה could be read as allowing a light divider, it does not teach that a solid wall is required. Our משנה is needed to teach that point.

keyTerms.meaning: A light partition, like a fence made of pegs

phrases.english: No, it refers to a mere light partition.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 18 by reading the later משנה differently.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The later משנה requires a real wall.
steps.terutzMaskana: The later משנה could mean only a light partition, so our משנה is needed to require a solid wall.

steps.title: Then the later משנה seems unnecessary
steps.stepSummary: Since our משנה teaches more, the גמרא asks why the later משנה is needed at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: Then let it teach this one and not teach that one!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now turns the question around. If our משנה teaches more, the later משנה seems unnecessary.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Our משנה teaches both that partners divide when they agree and that a solid wall is needed. That already covers the later משנה's ruling, so why does the later one exist?

keyTerms.meaning: Let it teach this one and not teach that one

phrases.english: Let it teach this one and not teach that one!
phrases.notes: "This one" is our משנה, and "that one" is the later משנה on 11a.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on step 19 and challenges whether the later משנה is needed.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Our משנה already covers its ruling and teaches more, so the later one seems extra.

steps.title: The later משנה is needed for holy books
steps.stepSummary: The later משנה was taught for its last clause: כתבי הקודש are not divided even if both partners want to divide them. This ends the alternative version.
steps.simpleTranslation: It needed the last clause: And holy books, even if both want to divide them, they do not divide them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the later משנה is needed for its last part, which teaches a new rule about holy books. This closes the second version of the discussion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling about agreement and division in the later משנה is only a lead-in. Its real new lesson is that a holy book must not be cut apart, even if both partners agree. That rule appears nowhere else, so the later משנה is needed.
steps.whatToRemember: Both versions reach the same structure. Our משנה teaches that agreeing partners must build a solid wall (here, because they made a קנין). The later משנה is needed for its rule that כתבי הקודש are never divided.

phrases.english: It needed the last clause:
and regarding holy books,
even if both of them want to,
they do not divide them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 20 and closes the second version.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The later clause is needed (סיפא אצטריכא ליה)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The later משנה adds nothing new.
steps.terutzMaskana: The later משנה is needed to teach that כתבי הקודש are never divided.

steps.title: If the courtyard cannot be divided by law, why can't they back out?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא recalls that our משנה is about a courtyard too small to be divided by force. It asks why their agreement should bind them at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: How did we set up our משנה? As a courtyard that has no law of division. But if so, what does it matter that they wanted to divide? Let them change their minds!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the case of the משנה. If no one can be forced to divide a small courtyard, a simple wish to divide should not stop either partner from backing out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier steps established that our משנה speaks of a small courtyard that is split only because both partners agreed. The problem is that a bare agreement is just words. So why does the משנה say they must build the wall?

keyTerms.meaning: You set up the case as
The law that lets one partner force a division
So what? What difference does it make?
Let them back out of it

phrases.english: In what case did you set up our משנה?
Where it has no law of division.
If it has no law of division,
then if they wanted to, so what?
Let them back out!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי בְּשֶׁאֵין בָּהּ דִּין חֲלוּקָהּ, כִּי רָצוּ מַאי הָוֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the alternative version ends, the גמרא returns to the main reading of the משנה, a small courtyard divided by agreement, and challenges it.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that partners of a small courtyard who agreed to divide must build a wall
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A verbal wish has no binding force when there is no law of division, so either side should be able to retract.

steps.title: They made a binding קנין
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן answers that the partners sealed their agreement with a קנין, so neither can back out.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אסי said in the name of רבי יוחנן: It is a case where they made a קנין with each other.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the משנה speaks of partners who made a formal act of acquisition, which made the deal binding.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Words alone can be taken back, but a קנין makes an agreement legally final. So the משנה's case is not just agreement but agreement locked in by a קנין.

keyTerms.meaning: They made a formal act of acquisition with them
An אמורא who transmits teachings of רבי יוחנן

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי אַסִּי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Asi said that Rabbi Yochanan said:
Where they made a kinyan with each other.
phrases.notes: A קנין is a formal act, like handing over a cloth, that makes a deal binding.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אַסִּי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: שֶׁקָּנוּ מִיָּדָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 22 by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The partners only agreed verbally, so they could retract.
steps.terutzMaskana: They sealed the agreement with a קנין, so it is binding.

steps.title: A קנין on mere words does not work
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges that a קנין cannot bind a promise to act. It must transfer something real.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if they made a קנין, so what? It is only a קנין on words!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer. A קנין that only commits someone to do something in the future is not a real קנין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A קנין works by transferring an actual object or property. An agreement to divide and build a wall is just a promise, which is called קנין דברים and has no force. So the problem of step 22 comes back.

keyTerms.meaning: A קנין on mere words or promises, which does not take effect

steps.confusionAlert: קנין דברים does not mean a spoken קנין. It means a קנין whose subject is only a promise, with no actual thing being transferred.

phrases.english: And if they made a kinyan, so what?
It is merely a kinyan on words!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 23.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's answer that they made a קנין
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A קנין on an obligation to act, with no property transferred, is invalid, so the partners could still retract.

steps.title: The קנין was on the actual sides of the courtyard
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the קנין set who gets which side, so it transferred real land.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a case where they made a קנין about the sides, meaning who takes which part.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that the קנין was not just a promise to divide. It fixed which part of the courtyard each partner would own.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the קנין assigned real pieces of land, it is a true transfer of property and not קנין דברים. Once each owns a fixed part, the duty to build the wall follows.

keyTerms.meaning: Sides or directions, which part of the courtyard each one gets

phrases.english: Where they made a kinyan regarding the sides.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 24.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining what the קנין was on
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The קנין was only on the promise to divide.
steps.terutzMaskana: The קנין assigned specific sides of the courtyard, a real transfer of land.

steps.title: Each partner took possession of his own part
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי gives another way the deal became binding: each partner did an act of ownership in his own section.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: For example, this one walked into his part and took possession, and that one walked into his part and took possession.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי offers a different case. Each partner acquired his section through חזקה, an act showing ownership.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of a קנין done by handing over an object, here each partner acquires his land directly by acting as its owner. Either way the division is completed on real property, so neither can back out.

keyTerms.meaning: Took possession through an act of ownership (חזקה)

steps.whatToRemember: The partners of a small courtyard are bound to build the wall only when their division was finalized on real land, either through a קנין on the sides or through each one's חזקה on his part.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
For example, this one walked within his own part
and took possession,
and that one walked within his own part and took possession.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר: כְּגוֹן שֶׁהָלַךְ זֶה בְּתוֹךְ שֶׁלּוֹ וְהֶחֱזִיק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second answer to the challenge of step 24.
steps.terutzMaskana: Each partner acquired his section through חזקה, completing the division on real land.

steps.title: Defining the four building materials
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about local building custom and explains גויל, גזית, כפיסין and לבנים.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: In a place where they are used to building, and so on. גויל means stones that are not smoothed. גזית means smoothed stones, as the verse says: 'All these were costly stones, cut to the measure of גזית.' כפיסין are small bricks. לבנים are large bricks.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next line of the משנה and explains the names of the building materials it lists.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says the wall is built with whatever material is local custom. The גמרא now identifies each one, and brings a verse to prove that גזית means stones that were cut and smoothed.

phrases.english: A place where they are accustomed to build, etc.
Gevil means stones that are not smoothed.
Gazit means stones that are smoothed,
as it is written:
"All these were costly stones,
according to the measures of cut stone (etc.)"
phrases.notes: מלכים א 7:9. Some versions leave out the word in round brackets.

phrases.english: Kefisin means small bricks.
Leveinin means large bricks.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the question of binding agreement to the next clause of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: גויל is unsmoothed stone, גזית is smoothed stone (proven from a verse), כפיסין are small bricks, and לבנים are large bricks.

steps.title: Maybe גויל means half-width smoothed stones
steps.stepSummary: רבה בריה דרבא asks how we know גויל means rough stones. Perhaps it means thin smoothed stones built in two rows with a gap.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה son of רבא said to רב אשי: How do we know that גויל means unsmoothed stones, and that the extra handbreadth is for the jutting edges? Maybe it is half a גזית stone, and the extra handbreadth is for the space between the rows.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בריה דרבא challenges the definition of גויל. He suggests another explanation that also accounts for why a גויל wall is one handbreadth thicker than a גזית wall.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה makes a גויל wall six טפחים and a גזית wall five. רב אשי's reading explains the extra טפח as room for rough stones sticking out. רבה offers a rival reading: two rows of thin smoothed stones with a one-טפח gap between them, so the definition is not yet proven.

keyTerms.meaning: The jutting edges of rough stones

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבָּה בְּרֵיהּ דְּרָבָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Rabba son of Rava said to Rav Ashi:

phrases.aramaic: מִמַּאי דִּגְוִיל אַבְנֵי דְּלָא מְשַׁפְּיָא נִינְהוּ,
phrases.english: From where do you know that gevil is unsmoothed stones,
and that this extra handbreadth
phrases.notes: The משנה gives a גויל wall six טפחים, one more than a גזית wall's five.

phrases.english: is for the jutting edges?
Perhaps it is half of a gazit stone,
and this extra handbreadth
is for the space between the rows;
phrases.notes: He pictures two thin rows of stone side by side, with a handbreadth gap between them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבָּה בְּרֵיהּ דְּרָבָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי: מִמַּאי דִּגְוִיל אַבְנֵי דְּלָא מְשַׁפְּיָא נִינְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the definition of גויל given in step 27.
steps.kashyaTarget: The definition of גויל as unsmoothed stones
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Another reading, thin smoothed stones in two rows with a gap, explains the extra טפח just as well, so the definition is not proven.

steps.title: Backing up the challenge with the case of כפיסין
steps.stepSummary: רבה בריה דרבא supports his reading of גויל by pointing to כפיסין. Everyone agrees that the extra טפח of a כפיסין wall is the gap between two rows of small bricks, so the same could be true of גויל.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is like what we say about bricks: כפיסין are small bricks and לבנים are large bricks, and the extra handbreadth in a כפיסין wall is the space between the two rows.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בריה דרבא is finishing his question from the last step. He brings a parallel to show his alternative reading of גויל makes sense.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, a כפיסין wall is one טפח thicker than a לבנים wall. We explain that the extra טפח is the gap between two rows of small bricks. In the same way, a גויל wall is one טפח thicker than a גזית wall, so maybe that extra טפח is also a gap between two rows of thin stones.

keyTerms.meaning: the extra handbreadth of wall thickness
between the rows; the gap between two rows of building material

phrases.english: As we say: kefisin are small bricks,
leveinin are large bricks,
and this extra handbreadth is for the space between the rows!
phrases.notes: In the משנה, a wall of כפיסין is 4 טפחים thick and a wall of לבנים is 3, so there is one extra טפח to explain.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the challenge of step 28 by bringing a parallel case as support.
steps.raayaObject: The alternative reading that גויל means thin smoothed stones built in two rows with a gap
steps.raayaSupportSource: The accepted explanation of כפיסין, where the extra טפח is the gap between rows

steps.title: The meanings are known by tradition
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that the meaning of כפיסין is not proven from the text either. It is a received tradition, and so is the meaning of גויל as rough, unsmoothed stones.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: By your logic, how do we know that כפיסין are small bricks? We know it from a tradition. In the same way, we know from a tradition that גויל means unsmoothed stones.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי answers the challenge. He says these word meanings are not worked out by logic. They were passed down as a tradition.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge used כפיסין as a model for reading גויל. רב אשי points out that the meaning of כפיסין itself rests only on tradition. If tradition decides there, it can also decide that גויל means rough stones, even though the text alone could be read either way.

keyTerms.meaning: and according to your reasoning; turns the questioner's own logic back on him
they learned it as a received tradition

steps.whatToRemember: The meanings of גויל and כפיסין are not proven from the wording. They come from a tradition passed down by the Sages.

phrases.english: He said to him: And according to your reasoning,
phrases.notes: The one speaking is רב אשי, answering רבה בריה דרבא.

phrases.english: that kefisin are small bricks, from where do we know it?
Rather, they learned it as a tradition;
so too, that gevil means unsmoothed stones,
they learned it as a tradition.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of steps 28–29.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Appeal to received tradition: the parallel used as proof rests on tradition too
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the extra טפח of כפיסין is a gap between rows, גויל might also be two rows of thin stones with a gap.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both definitions come from tradition, and the tradition says גויל means rough, unsmoothed stones.

steps.title: Another version: maybe כפיסין are rough stones
steps.stepSummary: In a second version, רב אחא בריה דרב אויא challenges the reading the other way. Maybe כפיסין are unsmoothed stones, and the extra טפח is room for their sticking-out edges, just as with גויל compared to גזית.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: רב אחא בריה דרב אויא said to רב אשי: How do you know that כפיסין are small bricks and the extra handbreadth is the gap between the rows? Maybe כפיסין are unsmoothed stones, and the extra handbreadth is for their sticking-out edges. That is like what we say: גויל means unsmoothed stones, גזית means smoothed stones, and the extra handbreadth is for the sticking-out edges!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a different version of the conversation. Here the question runs in reverse: it uses גויל to cast doubt on what כפיסין means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version, כפיסין was used to question גויל. Here גויל is used to question כפיסין. Since everyone explains the extra טפח of a גויל wall as room for the bumpy edges of rough stones, maybe the extra טפח of a כפיסין wall means the same thing, and כפיסין are rough stones too.

keyTerms.meaning: some say; introduces another version of the discussion
the sticking-out edges and corners of rough stones

steps.confusionAlert: This is the same argument as before, run in reverse. Before, כפיסין was the model used to question גויל. Now גויל is the model used to question כפיסין.

phrases.english: There are those who say:

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אַוְיָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Rav Aḥa son of Rav Avya said to Rav Ashi:
From where do you know that kefisin are small bricks,
and this extra handbreadth is for between the rows?

phrases.aramaic: דִּילְמָא מַאי כְּפִיסִין – אַבְנֵי דְּלָא מְשַׁפְּיָין,
phrases.english: Perhaps what are kefisin? Unsmoothed stones,
and this extra handbreadth is for the sticking-out edges;
as we say: gevil means unsmoothed stones,
gazit means smoothed stones,
and this extra handbreadth is for the sticking-out edges!
phrases.notes: A גויל wall is 6 טפחים thick and a גזית wall is 5, so here too there is one extra טפח.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְאָמְרִי, אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אַוְיָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second version of steps 28–30, in which the challenge runs in the opposite direction.
steps.kashyaTarget: The definition of כפיסין as small bricks, with the extra טפח as the gap between rows
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The accepted explanation of גויל (extra טפח for the bumpy edges of rough stones) could just as well explain כפיסין, so כפיסין might be rough stones.

steps.title: Again: the meaning is a tradition
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that the meaning of גויל as unsmoothed stones is also known only by tradition. So the meaning of כפיסין as small bricks is a tradition as well.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: By your logic, how do we know that גויל means unsmoothed stones? We know it from a tradition. Here too, we know it from a tradition.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי answers the second-version challenge the same way he answered the first. Both definitions come from a received tradition.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenger used גויל as his model. רב אשי shows that גויל's meaning is not proven from the text either, only from tradition. So tradition can just as well decide that כפיסין means small bricks.

keyTerms.meaning: here too; the same applies in this case

steps.whatToRemember: In both versions, the answer is the same. The meanings of the building words in the משנה (גויל, גזית, כפיסין, לבנים) are known from a received tradition, not worked out from the wording.

phrases.english: He said to him: And according to your reasoning,
that gevil means unsmoothed stones, from where do we know it?
Rather, they learned it as a tradition;
here too, they learned it as a tradition.
phrases.notes: He means the tradition that כפיסין are small bricks.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the second-version challenge of step 31.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Appeal to received tradition: the parallel used as proof rests on tradition too
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the extra טפח of גויל is for bumpy edges, כפיסין might also be rough stones.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both definitions come from tradition, and the tradition says כפיסין are small bricks.

steps.title: אביי learns that the gap between rows is always a handbreadth
steps.stepSummary: אביי draws a general building rule from the previous discussion: the space between the two rows of a wall is always one טפח.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: We can learn from this that the space between the two rows of a wall is always one handbreadth.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי takes the earlier explanation of כפיסין, which says the extra טפח is the gap between two rows of bricks, and turns it into a general rule for building walls.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier steps established that a כפיסין wall has an extra טפח because of the space between its two rows. אביי applies this more widely: wherever a wall is built in two rows, that inner space is one טפח.

keyTerms.meaning: Learn from it; we can conclude from this
The space between the rows of a wall
A handbreadth, a unit of measure

phrases.english: Abaye said: Learn from it:
every space between the rows is a handbreadth.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a general practical rule from the accepted meaning of כפיסין.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The gap between the two rows of a wall is one טפח.

steps.title: First version: the handbreadth rule is for mortar
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא limits אביי's rule. One טפח is enough when the gap is filled with טינא (mortar), but a gap filled with ריכסא (gravel) needs more space.
steps.simpleTranslation: This applies when the gap is filled with mortar. But when it is filled with gravel, more space is needed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא qualifies אביי's rule and explains when one טפח is enough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to this version, mortar holds the two rows together well, so a one-טפח gap is enough. Gravel binds less well, so a wider gap is needed.

phrases.english: This applies with mortar,
but with gravel, more is needed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the scope of אביי's rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A one-טפח gap is enough with mortar. Gravel needs more.

steps.title: Second version: the handbreadth rule is for gravel
steps.stepSummary: Another version reverses it. The one טפח is said about gravel, and mortar needs less than that.
steps.simpleTranslation: And some say: This applies with gravel. But with mortar, not that much space is needed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second version of the limit on אביי's rule, and it is the opposite of the first version.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this version, one טפח is the larger measure, needed for gravel. Mortar fills the gap well enough that even less than a טפח works. The two versions agree that mortar needs less space than gravel. They only disagree about which one the 'one טפח' refers to.

keyTerms.meaning: There are those who say; another version

steps.confusionAlert: Both versions agree that gravel needs more space than mortar. The only question is whether the 'one טפח' rule describes the mortar wall or the gravel wall.

phrases.english: And there are those who say:
this applies with gravel,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל בְּטִינָא לָא בָּעֵי כּוּלֵּי הַאי.
phrases.english: but with mortar, not that much is needed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposite version of the limit in step 34.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A one-טפח gap is needed with gravel. Mortar needs less.

steps.title: Challenge from the thin, tall wall in the first Temple
steps.stepSummary: Does a גזית wall really need five טפחים of thickness for every four אמות of height? The אמה טרקסין was thirty אמות high and only six טפחים thick, yet it stood.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that to say that with chiseled stone, for every four cubits of height, if the wall is five handbreadths thick it stands, and if not it does not stand? But there was the אמה טרקסין, which was thirty cubits high and only six handbreadths thick, and it stood!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the idea that a גזית wall needs a fixed thickness of five טפחים for every four אמות of height. It points to the wall inside the first מקדש as a counterexample.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If every four אמות of height needed five טפחים of thickness, a wall thirty אמות high would need to be far thicker than six טפחים. Yet the אמה טרקסין stood with only six. So the supposed rule seems wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that to say...? (introduces a doubtful conclusion)
The one-אמה-thick wall between the קודש הקדשים and the היכל in the first מקדש

phrases.english: Is that to say that with chiseled stone,
for every four cubits of height,
if the thickness is five handbreadths, it stands,
and if not, it does not stand?!
But there was the אמה טרקסין,
which was thirty cubits high,

phrases.aramaic: וְלָא הֲוָה פּוּתְיָא אֶלָּא שֵׁית פּוּשְׁכֵי;
phrases.english: and its thickness was only six handbreadths,
and it stood!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the gap between rows to the ratio of a wall's height to its thickness.
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption that a גזית wall needs five טפחים of thickness for every four אמות of height.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A real wall, the אמה טרקסין, stood at thirty אמות with only six טפחים of thickness, far less than that ratio would require.

steps.title: The extra handbreadth kept it standing
steps.stepSummary: Because the אמה טרקסין had one טפח more than five, it could stand even at that great height.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since there was an extra handbreadth, it stood.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The sixth טפח, one more than the basic five, is what let the אמה טרקסין stand so tall.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The five-טפחים rule is a minimum for an ordinary גזית wall. One additional טפח of thickness gives the wall enough extra strength to stand much higher, so the אמה טרקסין does not disprove the rule.

phrases.english: Since there is an extra handbreadth, it stands.
phrases.notes: Extra compared to the basic five טפחים: the אמה טרקסין had six.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the challenge from the אמה טרקסין.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the case: the counterexample had an additional טפח.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Six טפחים should not be enough for a thirty-אמה wall under the five-per-four ratio.
steps.terutzMaskana: The one extra טפח beyond five gives enough strength for a much taller wall.

steps.title: Why the second Temple had no אמה טרקסין
steps.stepSummary: If a six-טפחים wall could stand, why didn't they build an אמה טרקסין in the second מקדש?
steps.simpleTranslation: And in the second Temple, what is the reason they did not make an אמה טרקסין?
steps.whatsHappening: Building on the last answer, the גמרא asks why the second מקדש did not use the same kind of wall.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since we just learned that the six-טפחים wall worked, it is surprising that the second מקדש did not have one. The גמרא wants to know what was different.

phrases.english: And in the second Temple, what is the reason
that they did not make an אמה טרקסין?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows up on the answer about the extra טפח.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the second מקדש did not use a six-טפחים dividing wall.

steps.title: Six handbreadths only works up to thirty cubits
steps.stepSummary: A six-טפחים wall can stand only up to thirty אמות. The second מקדש was taller, so such a wall would not stand there.
steps.simpleTranslation: When it stands, it stands up to thirty cubits. More than that, it does not stand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the extra טפח only helps up to a height of thirty אמות. The second מקדש needed a taller divider.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This sets a limit on the answer in step 37. The extra טפח helps, but only up to thirty אמות. Since the second מקדש was taller, a six-טפחים wall would have fallen.
steps.whyThisMatters: This answer assumes the second מקדש was taller than the first, which the גמרא now sets out to prove.

phrases.english: When it stands, it stands up to thirty,
phrases.notes: Thirty אמות high, the height of the אמה טרקסין.

phrases.english: more than that, it does not stand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 38.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A six-טפחים wall stands only up to thirty אמות, and the second מקדש was taller.

steps.title: How do we know the second Temple was taller?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for a source that the second מקדש was taller than the first.
steps.simpleTranslation: And from where do we know that it was taller?
steps.whatsHappening: The last answer depended on the second מקדש being taller, so the גמרא asks for a source for that fact.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The explanation for the missing אמה טרקסין only works if the second מקדש really was higher. The גמרא wants a source before relying on it.

phrases.english: And from where do we know that it was taller?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the assumption behind step 39.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source that the second מקדש was taller than the first.

steps.title: The verse: the latter house will be greater
steps.stepSummary: The source is the פסוק in חגי that the glory of the latter house will be greater than the former.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'The glory of this latter house shall be greater than that of the former.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק saying the second מקדש would be 'greater' than the first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says the latter house will be greater, but it does not say in what way. The next step shows that not everyone reads 'greater' as meaning size.

keyTerms.meaning: The latter house, meaning the second מקדש

phrases.english: As it is written: 'Greater shall be the glory of this house,'
phrases.notes: חגי 2:9

phrases.english: 'the latter one, than the former one.'

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּכְתִיב גָּדוֹל יִהְיֶה כְּבוֹד הַבַּיִת הַזֶּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the request for a source in step 40.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A פסוק in חגי says the latter house will be greater than the former.

steps.title: A dispute over what 'greater' means
steps.stepSummary: רב and שמואל, or in another version רבי יוחנן and רבי אלעזר, disagree. One says 'greater' means in the building itself, and the other begins his view, which continues past this point.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב and שמואל disagree, and some say it was רבי יוחנן and רבי אלעזר. One said: greater in its building. And the other said:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that the meaning of the פסוק is disputed. One opinion reads 'greater' as referring to the size of the building, and the other opinion continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only the opinion that reads 'greater' as 'in the building' supports the claim that the second מקדש was taller. The second opinion is cut off here and will offer another meaning.

keyTerms.meaning: And some say it was (a different pair of names)

steps.confusionAlert: The amud ends in the middle of the second opinion. The dispute finishes on the next amud.

phrases.english: Rav and Shmuel disagree about this;

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לַהּ רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן וְרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר;
phrases.english: and some say it was Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar.
One said: greater in its building,
and one said:

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב וּשְׁמוּאֵל וְאָמְרִי לַהּ רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן וְרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that the meaning of the פסוק quoted in step 41 is disputed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One opinion reads 'greater' as greater in the building itself. The other opinion follows.
